text_blocks.snippet: Early signs of type 2 diabetes often develop slowly over months or years, making them easy to miss. According to the Mayo Clinic and the Cleveland Clinic, common early warning signs include:

list.snippet: Increased thirst and frequent urination: High blood sugar forces your kidneys to work overtime to filter and absorb excess glucose, causing you to pee more often—especially at night—and feel constantly thirsty.
Fatigue and weakness: When your cells cannot effectively absorb glucose for energy, you may experience persistent exhaustion, brain fog, or low energy.
Increased hunger: You may feel hungry shortly after eating because your body's cells are starved of the fuel they need.
Blurred vision: Excess sugar in the blood can cause fluid to shift into the lenses of your eyes, temporarily changing their shape and making your vision fuzzy.

Slow-healing sores or frequent infections: High blood sugar impairs circulation and weakens immune responses, making cuts, bruises, skin infections, urinary tract infections (UTIs), or yeast infections take longer to heal.
Tingling or numbness: Peripheral nerve damage from high blood sugar can cause a pins-and-needles sensation, burning, or numbness in the hands or feet.
Darkened skin patches (acanthosis nigricans): Velvety, dark patches of skin—frequently appearing on the neck, armpits, or groin—can be an early marker of insulin resistance.

Unexplained weight changes: Some individuals experience sudden, unintended weight loss as the body starts burning fat and muscle for energy, while others may experience weight gain linked to insulin resistance.

text_blocks.snippet: If you or someone you know is experiencing these symptoms, the safest next step is to schedule a visit with a doctor for a simple blood test (such as a fasting blood glucose or A1c test) to get an accurate diagnosis.
